faq.q: Why is there a vacuum in a flask?
faq.a: A vacuum has almost no particles, and conduction and convection both need particles to carry heat. So the vacuum gap blocks two of the three ways heat escapes.

faq.q: Why are the walls of a flask silvered?
faq.a: Shiny surfaces reflect infrared radiation. The silvering bounces heat rays back towards the drink instead of letting them cross the gap.
asks: Why is a flask shiny inside?

faq.a: Without it, hot air and steam would rise out of the top by convection and evaporation. Most of the heat a flask does lose leaks through the stopper and neck.
asks: What is the lid of a flask for?

faq.q: Can a flask keep drinks cold too?
faq.a: Yes. A flask does not make heat; it just slows heat moving in either direction. So it keeps cold drinks cold by stopping warmth getting in.
asks: Does a thermos work for cold drinks?

faq.a: The Scottish scientist James Dewar invented it in 1892 to keep chemicals very cold in his laboratory. A German company later sold it as the Thermos.

facts: Scottish scientist James Dewar invented the vacuum flask in 1892.
Thermos began as the brand name of a German company founded in 1904 to sell vacuum flasks.
